title: Karmic tail 6-20-14 in the destiny matrix: “the Victim”, three angels and a cup that flows both ways

seo.title: Karmic Tail 6-20-14 “The Victim” in the Destiny Matrix
seo.description: 6-20-14: love given in advance and years of waiting to be noticed. A ten-second date check, why no one born in December has it, and The Little Mermaid’s way out.
queries: what 6 20 14 means in the destiny matrix

short: 6-20-14 is the karmic tail that popular destiny matrix readings call “the Victim”, “the Sacrificial Soul” or “the Sacrificed Soul”. Its script: a person loves by giving. They give way, pull for two, put their own needs off “for later” — and silently wait for someone to see it, value it and pay it back. Most often nobody sees. Then they either give even more or one day present the bill: “after everything I’ve done for you”. The Lovers (6) open the circle: love you feel you have to earn. Judgement (20) holds it: waiting for the day when everything you gave is finally counted. The root is Temperance (14): an angel who holds both cups and pours water between them. Giving and receiving have to end up in the same hands. Everyone with this tail has the Wheel of Fortune (10) in the centre of the chart — the belief that good comes back on its own. The tail is rare: one birth date in 96, 22nd place out of 26. People born in December never have it. And it is the only one of the 26 tails that brings together all three “angel” cards of the Waite deck.

sections.h2: Do you have the 6-20-14 tail: a ten-second check
paragraphs: You don’t need a calculator. The tail depends on one number — the sum of the first three arcana of the matrix — and for 6-20-14 it must be exactly 14.

ol: **Day arcanum** — your day of birth. If it is greater than 22, add its digits: 23 → 5, 25 → 7, 30 → 3.
**Year arcanum** — the sum of the digits of the year. If it is greater than 22, add the digits again: 1985 → 23 → 5, 2000 → 2.

paragraphs: Add up the three numbers. If you get **14**, you have 6-20-14. There is no other way to get this tail.

ul: 01.12.2000: 1 + 12 + 2 = 15 → not this one either. December never gives less than 15, in any year.

paragraphs: Where the rule comes from. A sum of 14 puts D = 14 in the bottom corner of the chart. The centre is E = 14 + 14 = 28 → 10. The entry of the tail is M = D + E = 14 + 10 = 24 → 6, and the middle is N = D + M = 14 + 6 = 20. You cannot reach 14 by reducing a bigger number: the sum of the three numbers is never above 56, and the digits of any number from 23 to 56 add up to 13 at most. So the tail has no backup sums — only 14. We checked the rule against every day from 1900 to 2100 on the calculator’s engine.
The Lovers stand at the entry of five tails, and one more tail shares its centre and middle with 6-20-14. What sets them apart is the sum of the three numbers:
This arithmetic explains a few things that are not obvious:

ul: **It is a rare tail.** Of the 46,021 dates from 1900 to 2025, 480 give 6-20-14 — 1.04%. That is 22nd place out of 26. Only 21-10-7, 3-13-10, 9-18-9 and 6-14-8 are rarer.

**It is a 21st-century tail.** Among 20th-century dates it falls on one in 162; among dates since 2000, on one in 37 — more than four times as often. More than half of all 6-20-14 dates since 1900 fall in 2000–2025. The record year is 2000: 20 dates. The reason is that the tail needs a small sum. Years of the 20th century have a large arcanum (1975 → 22), and the sum almost always shoots past 14. Years of the 21st century have a small one (2000 → 2, 2010 → 3).

**There is a generation that does not have it at all.** Not a single date from 1921 to 1948 gives 6-20-14: the arcanum of those years runs from 13 to 22, so the sum is above 14 from the start. In the whole of the 1920s the tail came up once — on 1 January 1920. After that the gaps get shorter: 1950–1957, 1960–1966, 1970–1975, 1980–1984, 1990–1993. Since 1994 the tail has come up every year, and the first year without it will be 2029.

**Never in December.** The month number is part of the sum, and December gives at least 1 + 12 + 2 = 15. Nobody born in December between 1900 and 2100 has 6-20-14. November gave it once in two hundred years — on 1 November 2000. October gave it three times between 1900 and 2025: 2 October 2000, 1 October 2001 and 1 October 2010. January, on the other hand, gives it often: among people born in January since 2000, one in sixteen has it.

**Never in the middle of the month either.** People born on the 12th to the 22nd never get the tail, in any year: the day arcanum is already too big. The 11th and the 29th gave it once each, both in 2000 — 11 and 29 January. 6-20-14 is most common among people born on the 1st.
**In some years, only on New Year’s Day.** In years with arcanum 12 — 1902, 1911, 1920, 2019, 2028 — the tail falls on exactly one date: 1 January.

**14-20-6 is the same tail.** If you see 14, 20 and 6 on the bottom ray of your chart, you are reading the same tail from the outer corner towards the centre. The method always writes it M–N–D, from the centre down. No tail in this scheme starts with 14 or 20: the inner point M is always a multiple of three. The roles do not depend on the reading direction: the Lovers are the entry, Temperance is the root.

paragraphs: Popular readings explain the name with a past life. The legend comes in three versions. In the darkest one, the soul was sacrificed — in a ritual or for someone else’s plan. In another, the person sacrificed themselves: for their family, a loved one or “the common good”. In the third, they gave up their talent for someone’s sake. About the present life the same readings say something similar: the person gives more than they get, cannot ask directly, drops hints and waits for others to guess, and builds up resentment — “I’m there for everyone, and no one is there for me”. There is a mirror version too: the person grows up in a family that sacrifices for them and shields them from everything in the world. The legend cannot be checked: no birth date can reconstruct anyone’s past. But as a metaphor it is accurate. This is how a person lives when loving and giving themselves away are one and the same thing.

The Russian name has a twist that is easy to miss. The single word zhertva means two opposite things: what is offered up and the one who has been harmed. Prinesti zhertvu, “to make a sacrifice”, is something you do. Stat’ zhertvoy, “to become a victim”, is something you suffer. The names of the tail swing between these two meanings. “The Sacrificed Soul” is about the one who was given away. “The Sacrificial Soul” is about the one who gives. The 6-20-14 tail is precisely about how the second turns into the first: someone who gave for years one day finds that they are the one who got hurt. English splits these meanings between two words, sacrifice and victim. But victim, too, began at the altar: in the 15th century it meant an animal offered to a god, and only from the mid-17th century a person harmed by another.

Even more interesting is where the word comes from. Max Vasmer’s etymological dictionary traces zhertva to the Old Church Slavonic verb zhreti, “to offer a sacrifice” (the source of zhrets, “priest”, too). And it puts the word in one row with Lithuanian gìrti, “to praise”, Sanskrit gṛṇā́ti, “sings, praises”, Avestan gar, “praise, reward”, and Latin grātus, “pleasing, grateful”. **Hidden inside the word zhertva are praise, reward and gratitude.** That is the invisible half of the script: you give — and wait to be praised.

The Romans had a formula for this kind of exchange: do ut des, “I give so that you may give”. It described contracts in Roman law and vows to the gods: I promise an altar, a temple or games if my prayer is granted. There is nothing shameful in the formula. It is an honest exchange, and both sides know about it. The trouble with 6-20-14 is something else. **The sacrifice in this tail is a do ut des contract that only one side knows about.** The person gives and silently sets a condition. The other takes and has no idea they have signed a contract. When the term runs out, they are handed a bill they are hearing about for the first time.

sections.h2: Three angels: what this tail is made of
paragraphs: In the Waite deck, the one this article reads the cards by, a large angel appears on only three of the major arcana — the Lovers, Temperance and Judgement. Those are exactly the numbers of the 6-20-14 tail, and they never meet in any other tail. (The corners of the Wheel of Fortune, which sits in the centre for this tail, also show winged figures. But these, as Waite writes, are the four Living Creatures, not angels.) Popular readings promise people with 6-20-14 a “guardian angel” and luck from above. There really are three angels in the tail. They just do different things.

On the sixth card the angel hovers above a man and a woman, arms spread wide, and, in Waite’s words, is **“pouring down influences”**. Love comes from above here, and it does not have to be earned. On the twentieth card the angel blows a trumpet and the dead rise from their tombs. On the fourteenth the angel is alone, with no people nearby. It stands with one foot on land and the other in water and pours water from cup to cup. Our reading: the 6-20-14 tail is the angel’s path from the sky into the person’s own hands. At the start, love pours down on you. At the end, you hold both cups.

The most surprising thing is that Waite himself links the middle of this tail with its root. The twentieth card, he writes, **“has been called truly in the past a card of eternal life, and for this reason it may be compared with that which passes under the name of Temperance”**. And of the fourteenth he says that it holds some part of the secret of eternal life — **“as it is possible to man in his incarnation”**. So the tail holds two eternities. One comes after the trumpet, at the end of time. The other is possible now, in this life. This is the main turn of 6-20-14: from a reward “later” to an exchange “now”.

sections.h2: How the circle works: an advance, waiting for judgement and two cups
paragraphs: **1. Entry: the Lovers — love you want to earn.** Waite calls the sixth card “in all simplicity the card of human love”. The man and the woman on it are **“unveiled before each other”**, like Adam and Eve in the first days of paradise. Benebell Wen points out a detail of the composition: the man looks at the woman, and the woman looks up, at the angel. A gaze on this card does not come back the way it went. Wen also writes that the Lovers carry a strong feeling of paradise at first, and that this feeling may turn out to be fleeting.

In 6-20-14 the entry reads like this: love feels like a gift that has to be justified. The person grows attached — to a partner, family, work, friends — and starts paying right away. They adapt, guess what others want, take things on, put their own needs aside. They try to hold on to paradise by giving. The stronger the love, the more the person is ready to give and the less they say about what it costs. The two on Waite’s card are unveiled before each other. Here the main thing stays hidden: how much was given and what is expected in return.

**2. Mechanism: Judgement — waiting for the day when it all counts.** On the twentieth card the angel blows a trumpet and the dead rise from their tombs. This is the Last Judgement — the day when every deed is named and everyone gets their due. The tail clings to exactly this picture. What you give is written into an invisible book, and you wait for the day it is read out loud. Your partner will realise how much they were given. The children will grow up and appreciate it. The boss will notice who really carried the department. “God sees everything.” “It will all be counted up there.” In the bitterest version: “when I’m dead, you’ll understand”.

But in Waite, the trumpet of Judgement does not sound from outside. The twentieth card, he writes, marks the accomplishment of the great work of transformation **“in answer to the summons of the Supernal—which summons is heard and answered from within”**. And he asks: what is that within us which sounds a trumpet, so that all that is lower in our nature rises in response? In the 6-20-14 tail the trumpet has been moved outside. Another person is appointed judge, and the verdict is supposed to be their gratitude. Wen says the twentieth card is about salvation. In this tail salvation is expected from outside. Or you save others so that one day someone will save you.

The day of judgement never comes: the other person does not know that a trial has even been scheduled. So the person passes the verdict themselves. There are two options. “They are ungrateful” — and the Victim becomes the Accuser. “So I didn’t give enough” — and the Victim gives even more. Wen describes reversed Judgement as an error of judgement: the person has misread the facts and come to the wrong conclusion. Both of the tail’s verdicts are exactly that. The person thinks their contribution was not valued. Most often, nobody even knew about it.

**3. Root: Temperance — both cups in your own hands.** On Waite’s fourteenth card a winged angel, neither male nor female, is **“pouring the essences of life from chalice to chalice”**. It has one foot on the earth and the other on the water. When this principle rules our consciousness, Waite writes, it “tempers, combines and harmonises” the psychic and material natures. The card’s divinatory list reads almost like a housekeeping one: “economy, moderation, frugality, management, accommodation”.

Look at the angel’s hands. Both cups are its own. In sacrifice everything works differently. The person holds one cup, their own, and pours from it into someone else’s. The second cup is held by the other person, and only they decide whether to pour anything back. The root task of 6-20-14 is to take the second cup into your own hands. The second cup is not someone else’s life to manage but your own “receiving”. The task is not to stop giving but to run the exchange yourself. To know how much you can give. To say what you need. And to be able to accept.

P. D. Ouspensky, a Russian author who wrote about the Tarot before the revolution, calls the fourteenth card not Temperance but Time. In his book “The Symbolism of the Tarot” the angel holds a gold cup and a silver one, and the Voice explains: **“One of the cups the angel holds is the past, the other is the future. The rainbow stream between the cups is the present. You see that it flows both ways.”** And further on: people think that everything keeps flowing in one direction. In a later edition of the book the narrator admits that he watched the stream and could not tell from which cup it was flowing into which. Wen quotes these words of Ouspensky in her book as well: she notes that several notable twentieth-century texts call Temperance “the Time card”. In the same place she writes about the stream itself: there is a question of whether the water flows from the higher cup to the lower, with gravity, or from the lower to the higher, against the laws of physics.
For this tail, this is the key sign. **In sacrifice it is always clear which way it flows: from me to you. In Temperance you cannot tell — the stream flows both ways.**

It is just as important to see what the root does not ask of you. Waite notes that the picture on the card, strictly speaking, “has no especial connexion with Temperance”, and that the name hides another, deeper meaning. For 6-20-14 this is the key. Temperance here is not “give a little less”, and it is not stinginess. It is the skill of mixing: your own and other people’s, giving and taking, earth and water. Wen calls the fourteenth card “the healing card”. In relationships, according to Wen, it calls for tempering extreme emotions, and resentment is named among them outright.

**4. The wheel keeps turning.** Until the root is lived through, the circle repeats: a new attachment — a new advance — a new wait for judgement. With each turn the stakes rise. The more you have given, the scarier it is to admit that nobody was keeping count. That is why people with this tail often stay where they stopped being noticed long ago: leaving means writing off the investment.
**Signs that the circle has started a new turn:**

ul: you said “it’s no trouble” when it was;
you helped when nobody asked, and now you are waiting to see if anyone notices;
instead of a request — a sigh, a hint or “never mind, I’ll do it myself”;
in a fight you bring up what you once gave;
it feels awkward to accept a gift until you have given one back;
you let yourself rest only when you truly can’t go on.

sections.h2: Rescuer, Victim and Accuser — one and the same tail
paragraphs: In 1968 the American psychiatrist Stephen Karpman described the “drama triangle” — three roles people cycle through in tangled relationships: the Rescuer, the Victim and the Persecutor. He drew the roles from fairy tales, above all from Little Red Riding Hood. The 6-20-14 tail goes through all three — often in a single evening.

head: Rescuer
Victim
Accuser
Tail worked through
rows: put up with it and wait to be noticed
“I’m there for everyone, and no one is there for me”
“I’ll help with this, not with that”, “I need help”
pour from their own into someone else’s
their own is empty, waiting to be filled
hasn’t started yet: “I don’t need anything”
resentment and a life on hold

paragraphs: Here is what it looks like in real life. She volunteered to collect her mother’s things from the dacha, the family’s country house — Rescuer. She hauled boxes for three hours while her brother “was busy” — Victim. In the evening she told him on the phone: “Of course, you always have something on, and I work like a horse” — Accuser. In the morning she is ashamed of her tone and offers to go alone again next time. The circle has closed, and nobody ever asked her brother whether he was free on Saturday.

The tail has a flip side that popular readings mention less often. A person with 6-20-14 may grow up as the one others sacrifice for: they are looked after, decisions are made for them, they are given the last of everything. Such a child learns early that love is when someone suffers for you. Later they either expect the same from a partner or start suffering for others themselves. The roles in the triangle change, but the triangle stays.

In 1990 the transactional analyst Acey Choy proposed the “winner’s triangle” — a way out of each role. Instead of the Victim — vulnerability: saying directly what you need and that you are struggling. Instead of the Rescuer — caring: helping when asked and not doing for others what they can do themselves. Instead of the Persecutor — assertiveness: speaking up about what bothers you without punishing anyone. All three skills fit into one picture of Temperance. Asking means holding out your own cup. Giving means pouring into someone else’s. Setting limits means knowing when to stop the stream.

sections.h2: The hidden fourth card: everyone with 6-20-14 has the Wheel of Fortune in the centre
paragraphs: Everyone who has this tail has 10, the Wheel of Fortune, in the centre of the matrix. It is arithmetic: the sum 14 plus the bottom corner 14 gives 28, and 28 reduces to 10. In the method, the centre of the chart is the comfort zone: what a person returns to when nothing is demanded of them. The entry of the tail is made up of the centre and the root: the Lovers of this tail are Temperance plus the Wheel, 14 + 10 = 24 → 6.

Wen opens her description of the tenth card with words that sound almost like a joke for a karmic tail: **“Key 10: Wheel of Fortune is the karma card”**. What goes up will come down. What hits bottom will bounce up. History repeats itself, and there is a sense of déjà vu. The 6-20-14 tail literally has the karma card in its centre. Our reading: the comfort zone of this tail is karma as bookkeeping. “Good comes back.” “What goes around comes around.” “You reap what you sow.” If you invest enough in people, the wheel is bound to pay out some day. And when it doesn’t, a bitter saying settles on the same axle: “no good deed goes unpunished”. Both phrases are the same belief: good is a deposit that should earn interest.

Waite is strict about such bookkeeping. Behind the symbol of the wheel, he writes, lies **“the denial of chance and the fatality which is implied therein”**. Neither “that’s how it turned out” nor “that’s just my fate”. Waite insists on one more detail: the sphinx must sit on the wheel itself, not on a separate pedestal above it. Otherwise the main idea is lost — **“stability amidst movement”**. The wheel turns, the figures on the rim rise and fall, and the sphinx stays put. That is the task of the centre for 6-20-14. While you are on the rim, you rise when you are thanked and fall when you go unnoticed. In the sphinx’s place, your worth does not depend on how this turn played out.

Of the reversed Wheel, Wen writes something that sounds like a prescription for this tail. It is a person who **cannot rely on external forces to sweep in and carry them**: they will have to put in their own willpower and swim against the current. Wen recalls the legend of the koi that swam up a waterfall and became a dragon. A calculated number is never reversed, but the hint points in the right direction. For 6-20-14, swimming against the current of karma means no longer waiting for the wheel to repay the debt by itself — and asking instead.

The Wheel appears in this chart twice: in the centre and in the personal purpose (more on this below). One card, two roles. In the comfort zone the person rides the rim. In the purpose they take the sphinx’s place.

sections.h2: A fairy tale that reads like this tail
paragraphs: There is a fairy tale everyone read as a child and few reread as adults — Hans Christian Andersen’s “The Little Mermaid” (1837). The parallel is ours, not part of the method’s tradition. But there are so many matches that it is impossible to pass it by.

The youngest mermaid wants an immortal soul. Her grandmother explains how to get one: a human must love the mermaid so much that she becomes **“dearer to him than his father and mother”**, and have a priest join their hands — **“then a part of his soul will pass into you… He will give you a soul and keep his own”**. Remember this sentence. It is a formula for an exchange in which nobody loses anything: one gives, and their own cup does not run dry.

But the little mermaid hears something else: a soul can be bought. She swims to the sea witch, who names the price: “You have a lovely voice… but you must give that voice to me.” — “If you take my voice, what will I have left?” — “Your beautiful face, your graceful walk and your speaking eyes.” The witch brews the potion with her own blood and, as payment, cuts out the little mermaid’s tongue. Even the ritual from the tail’s legend is here.

Then comes the whole circle of 6-20-14. Every step feels to the little mermaid as if she were **“treading on sharp knives”**, yet she dances for the prince better than anyone. He calls her his “little foundling” and lets her sleep on a velvet cushion outside his door. He loves her, Andersen writes, **“only as one loves a dear, good child”**. She watches the slave girls sing and thinks: “Oh, if only he knew that I gave up my voice forever just to be near him!” He tells her about the girl from the temple who supposedly saved him after the shipwreck, and the little mermaid sighs to herself: “Alas! He doesn’t know that it was I who saved his life!”

Then the judgement comes, but the verdict goes to someone else. The ship sails into the harbour of the neighbouring kingdom, and horns sound from the high towers. When the princess finally arrives, the prince recognises her as the girl from the temple and cries out: **“It’s you! You saved my life when I lay half-dead on the seashore!”** And to the little mermaid he says: **“You will rejoice in my happiness, for you love me so much!”** At the wedding she carries the bride’s train.

Last comes the fork of the Lovers in its darkest form. The sisters gave their hair to the witch and brought a knife: “Either he or you — one of you must die before sunrise!” The sacrifice script knows no other way out: either give yourself up or destroy the other. The little mermaid throws the knife into the waves and turns into sea foam. In the morning the prince and his bride search the ship for her: **“Sadly they gazed at the heaving foam, as if they knew that the little mermaid had thrown herself into the waves.”** The fantasy “when I’m dead, you’ll understand” came true to the letter — and changed nothing.

Compare the tale with the cards. The angel of Temperance stands with one foot on land and the other in water. The little mermaid had to choose between sea and land, and she paid for the land with the sea. The trumpet of Judgement is a voice, the one that calls and names. That was the first thing the little mermaid gave away. And the root of the tail was spoken by the grandmother at the very start of the tale: give a soul and keep your own.

Andersen does not leave his heroine in the foam. She rises to the daughters of the air, and they explain: a mermaid has no immortal soul, and **“her eternal existence depends on the will of another”**. You could not describe the middle of this tail more precisely: a person’s worth is in someone else’s hands. The daughters of the air themselves can earn a soul by doing good deeds for three hundred years. And then the tale has a sentence that makes an adult reader uneasy. If the daughters of the air find an obedient child in a house, their time is shortened by a year. If they find a naughty one, they weep, **“and every tear adds a day to our long time of trial”**. The economy of sacrifice goes on even in heaven — and is passed on to children: your behaviour makes an adult unhappy. Why it is better not to talk to children like this, see below.

And one detail that is easy to miss. Earlier Andersen notes that the little mermaid sighed but could not cry. Risen to the daughters of the air, she **“for the first time felt tears in her eyes”**. A feeling that could not be expressed before found a way out at last.

Every child who finishes the tale asks: why didn’t she write to the prince? Andersen gives no answer. The tail does: someone in the Victim role doesn’t tell, they wait for others to guess. In 1989 Disney rewrote the ending, and it is telling what the happy ending rests on: the mermaid gets her voice back, and by it the prince recognises who saved him. This story ends well only in the version where the voice is returned.

sections.h2: Where else 10, 20, 14 and 6 appear in your chart
paragraphs: Everyone with this tail has the same sum of the three numbers, so many other points of the matrix are the same too. Going through all dates from 1900 to 2025 gives this picture:

head: Where in the matrix
What everyone with 6-20-14 has
rows: Totals of the male (F + H) and female (G + I) ancestral lines

paragraphs: **All four purposes are the same for everyone.** Of the 26 tails, this happens in only four: 6-20-14, 3-13-10, 9-18-9 and 6-14-8. 6-20-14 is the most common of them. The reason is arithmetic. The purposes are calculated from the day, month, year and bottom corner, and in this tail the sum of the three numbers is fixed at 14, which leaves no room for variation. For example, the personal purpose is the reduced sum of the month and the bottom corner plus the sum of the day and the year. Whatever the date, it comes to 10.

**Two arcana of the tail come back as purposes.** The Wheel is both the comfort zone and the personal purpose. Judgement is both the mechanism of the tail and the social purpose. What follows is our reading, not a rule of the method. In the mechanism, Judgement is waiting for someone else’s verdict. In relationships with people it can ripen into the opposite: the ability to notice other people’s contribution and say it out loud. A person who waited for years to be noticed can become the one who notices others. Such people are rare, and it feels good to be around them.

**The Empress — abundance instead of self-giving.** Everyone with this tail has the Empress as their spiritual purpose. Waite sees in her **“above all things universal fecundity”**, “the fruitful mother of thousands”: a field of corn is ripening in front of her throne, and beyond it there is a fall of water. Put her next to Temperance. The angel measures out water from cup to cup, while the Empress’s water falls by itself, because there is plenty of it. This is not a mother’s role and not a hint about gender. It is an image of what a gift looks like when it comes from fullness rather than self-denial. In sacrifice a person gives the last they have. In abundance, they give what overflows the brim.

**Manipura: a will that relies on luck.** In Manipura, the chakra of will, status and money, everyone with 6-20-14 has the Wheel twice, with Judgement in the Emotions column. Our reading: here it is easy to live by “however it turns out” and “however they judge it”. What my work is worth will be decided by circumstances and by my boss. The worked-through version of the same chakra is naming your own price.

**Tail numbers that repeat.** Some holders of the tail have these three arcana in the chart once more. People born in June get the same trio on the sky line: 6-14-20. People born in years with arcanum 6 (1986, 1995, 2004, 2013, 2022) get it in Muladhara: 6-14-20. And for those born in 2002, 2011 and 2020 it sits in Svadhisthana (14-6-20), while the relationship line repeats the neighbouring tail — 6-8-20. For the date 04.06.2002 the trio 6, 14 and 20 appears in the chart three times.

**Sixty years.** On the age scale the bottom corner covers the years from 60 to 70, and everyone with this tail has Temperance there. At this age the exchange usually changes direction: a person still helps the younger ones and already needs help themselves. Both cups have to be held. All of this is a coincidence in the scheme, not a forecast and not information about health.

rows: the gratitude of the one you gave to

paragraphs: **With 15-20-5**, 6-20-14 shares the centre and the mechanism: the Wheel and Judgement. But the trumpet sounds differently. In 15-20-5 someone else’s voice calls you to revolt: you hear “you can’t do that” and you rise up against it. In 6-20-14 that voice is awaited as a reward: “tell me I’m good”. One tail answers another’s judgement with protest, the other with service.

**With 6-8-20** it shares the entry — the Lovers, and Judgement is in both tails. In 6-8-20 Judgement is the root, a call you have yet to arrive at, and Justice holds the circle: there a choice of the heart goes on trial, and the hearing drags on for years. In 6-20-14 Judgement stands in the middle: it is the waiting that holds the circle, and Temperance becomes the root. These tails also mirror each other. For people born in 2002, 2011 and 2020 with the 6-20-14 tail, the relationship line is 6-8-20. And for their peers with the 6-8-20 tail, the relationship line is 6-20-14.
The scenes below are made-up examples to illustrate the mechanism, not a portrait of everyone with this tail.

**Forty jars.** Every summer she puts up forty jars of pickles and pepper relish, though her children asked her long ago not to: they have nowhere to keep them and can’t eat that much. In autumn the jars sit untouched on the children’s balcony, and she sees it. “I spent all summer at the stove, and you don’t want it.” The jars are not about food. They are a contribution that has to be valued. Turning down the jars sounds to her like turning her down.

**The call that never came.** He never calls his parents first: “I don’t want to impose, they have their own lives.” And he stores up resentment: “They don’t care about me — not one call in a month.” Meanwhile his parents think he is busy and doesn’t want to be bothered. Two cups stand empty facing each other, and each is waiting to be filled.

The strong version in both scenes is the same — say it directly. “It matters to me when you take my jars. How about I make five jars, but of what you actually eat.” “I miss you, let’s talk on Sundays — I’ll be the one who calls.”
Everyone with 6-20-14 has a relationship line that starts with the same card as the tail — the Lovers. So love almost always passes through the question “how much am I ready to give?”

**Dinner at eight.** Their anniversary. He spent half the day cooking three dishes and said nothing: he wanted it to be a surprise. She came home at ten, tired, ate something standing up and went to bed. That night he thinks she doesn’t care. In the morning she learns about the anniversary from his icy silence. It is the same muteness as the little mermaid’s: he tried as hard as he could and didn’t say the main thing. The strong version would sound like this: “It’s our anniversary today, I’m cooking something. It matters to me that we sit down together at eight. Can you make it?”

**The move as a trump card.** She quit her job and followed him to another city when he was transferred. Nobody made her: she decided herself and didn’t even talk it over. Ten years later, one phrase comes up in every serious fight: “I gave up everything for you.” The sacrifice has turned into a trump card that beats any argument he makes. You can’t argue with it, and you can’t fix it either. This is what a do ut des that only one side knew about looks like: the condition appeared after the fact.

There is a reverse scene too. The partner of someone with 6-20-14 lives for years next to a person who asks for nothing, and gets used to that as normal. Then they are accused of being callous and genuinely don’t understand why. This tail makes the other person a debtor without their knowledge. The worked-through version is a union where both say out loud what they give and what they need. It is less romantic than sacrifice. But ten years later nobody presents a bill.

**The one who stays till nine.** He finishes his colleagues’ work, ties up other people’s loose ends on Friday evenings and never asks for a promotion. He is sure his manager sees who carries the department. The promotion goes to a colleague who simply walked in and asked. The tail’s verdict: “they don’t value people here.” He leaves — and at the new place it all starts again. The mechanism doesn’t need karma: a manager doesn’t see what nobody tells them.

**Free for friends.** She is very good at her craft but doesn’t charge people she knows — “it’s awkward”. Friends bring their friends. A year later half her work is free, and she is angry at people who don’t even suspect they are taking advantage of her kindness. Popular readings describe this as “I feel awkward asking to be paid for my work.” Here the Wheel sets the price: “whatever they give.” The worked-through version is to name the price herself and announce any discount as a gift: “Pay half — the rest is my gift.” Then the gift is visible and the exchange is fair.

The strength here is real. People with a worked-through 6-20-14 do well where things need connecting and restoring: in medicine and care, teaching, psychology, mediation, hospitality, in teams where the atmosphere matters. Temperance is the card of measure, and such people know the measure of a gift: how much help it takes to support someone without smothering them. These are directions, not a list of professions: you still choose by your interests and skills.

Popular readings attribute to this tail illnesses “for attention” and addictions. The tail makes no diagnoses, and there is more on this below, in the questions. But the script has two everyday habits that many people recognise.

**Rest only with a sick note.** A person lets themselves lie down in the middle of the day only with a fever. While they are healthy, resting feels shameful: “others have it worse.” Illness turns out to be the only permission to accept care.

**A well-earned reward.** “I do so much for everyone, I’ve earned it” — and in the evening, a third glass, a box of chocolates or a purchase nobody needs. The person can’t receive directly, so the reward sneaks in through the back door. Wen describes reversed Temperance as excess and an inability to curb cravings. A calculated number is never reversed, but the mechanism is recognisable: when the cup is empty, it gets topped up any old way.

Since 2000, one child in thirty-seven has had this tail, and among those born in January, one in sixteen. The tail says nothing about your family and does not predict that your child will be hurt. But if the tail’s script is love that has to be paid for by giving, the most useful thing parents can do is not to teach it.

ul: **Don’t turn care into a bill.** “I gave my life for you”, “we went without everything for your sake” — this is how a child learns that love is a debt. Care as much as you like, but don’t remind them what it cost.

**Don’t raise them with tears.** “Mum is crying because of you” — this is the logic of the ending of “The Little Mermaid”, where every tear a daughter of the air sheds over a naughty child adds a day to her trial. A child with 6-20-14 will learn this faster than others and will sacrifice themselves for years, just so that nobody cries.

**Respond to a direct request, not a hint.** If a child sulks and waits for you to guess, calmly say: “I can see you need something. Tell me in words.” A direct request should work better than sulking.
**Allow “no”.** A child is allowed not to share a favourite toy and not to kiss an aunt. Someone who couldn’t say no as a child gives everything away as an adult.
**Teach them to receive.** When a child is given a present, “thank you” is enough. No need for an instant “and what will you give back?”. Receiving is a skill too, and this tail needs it most of all.

sections.h2: Care or sacrifice: how to tell them apart

ul: Did anyone ask you to do this?
Does the person you are helping know what it costs you?
If nobody says thank you, will you regret doing it?
Will you bring it up in a fight?
If the answer to the last two questions is “yes”, it is not a gift but a contract that only you know about.
Is it clear who should help?
Is it clear what exactly is needed and when?
Can the answer be “no”?
“I’m so tired” is a hint. “Can you pick our son up from nursery today?” is a request.

paragraphs: **Giving way or dissolving:**

ul: Is there anything of yours in this decision?
Would you have suggested this option if you weren’t afraid of someone’s displeasure?
After giving way, did you feel lighter — or did the invisible book gain another line?

paragraphs: **Measure or self-denial:**

ul: Temperance is not “less for me”. It is a mix that holds both what is yours and what is theirs.
If among your last ten decisions there isn’t a single one where you chose yourself, that is not measure but self-denial.

sections.h2: What to do with the 6-20-14 tail: eight practices
paragraphs: These are the author’s exercises, drawn from the logic of the trio — not a ritual and not a promise of results.

ol: **Open the invisible book.** Write down what you gave over the past year without being asked — time, money, energy, concessions — and what you are silently expecting in return. For each line, choose one of two: ask for it out loud, or write it off for good and count it as a gift. There is no third option — waiting longer — on the list.

**One direct request a day.** The formula is simple: “I need… Can you…?” — no preamble, no excuses and no “if it’s not too much trouble”. Hints don’t count. This is the voice the little mermaid gave away first, and you get it back through practice.

**A pause before “yes”.** Don’t answer any request straight away: “I’ll let you know tonight.” In that time, ask yourself: am I agreeing because I want to, or because I’m afraid they’ll stop loving me otherwise?

**Name the exchange.** Before you help, say what it is. “This is a gift, I don’t need anything” — and really expect nothing. Or: “I’ll help with the move, and on Saturday you look after my kids.” Do ut des is no sin if both sides know about it.

**Accept without giving change.** When someone gives you something or helps you, say “thank you” — and that’s it. No “oh, you shouldn’t have” and no instant favour in return. The French sociologist Marcel Mauss wrote in “The Gift” (1925) that the gift rests on three obligations: to give, to receive and to give back. In archaic societies, refusing to give, like refusing to receive, meant refusing an alliance. “I don’t need anything” sounds modest, but by this logic it is a closed door.

**Say it ten seconds sooner.** “That hurts”, “this matters to me”, “I can’t do it like this” — in the moment, not after a month of silence. Hurt voiced right away is information for the other person. Hurt stored up for a year is a verdict.

**A cup for yourself.** Once a week, do something just for yourself — without first having to get exhausted, fall ill or finish everything else. Rest that has to be earned is the same sacrifice, only made to yourself.

**The family legend of sacrifice.** Remember who in your family was praised for self-sacrifice and in what words: “lived her whole life for others”, “nothing for herself, everything for the children”. Decide what you take from this story — care, loyalty, generosity — and what you leave behind: the rule “love is proved by giving yourself up”.

paragraphs: If you have become a victim in the literal sense — of violence, threats, humiliation, financial control — it is not about the tail or your “programme”. It is not a lesson to be lived through but a situation that calls for real help: from people close to you, a lawyer, a psychologist, a crisis line.

sections.h2: The strength of 6-20-14: a person who knows the measure of a gift
paragraphs: In its worked-through version this tail gives a rare combination. The person can love seriously and generously (the Lovers). They can see and name other people’s contribution — the very thing they once waited for themselves (Judgement). And they can mix: their own with others’, asking with helping, earth with water (Temperance). Others feel lighter around such people — not because they do everything for them, but because they give exactly as much as is needed. They make good hosts, teachers, doctors, and the friends people turn to on a hard day. Popular readings promise this tail that the person “will be able to ask those around them for anything they want, and will get it”. This is not magic. It is what happens to anyone who starts asking directly: people like helping those who say how to help.

“The Little Mermaid” has a sentence that suits this tail better than any spell. The grandmother says it, long before the witch, the knives and the foam: **“He will give you a soul and keep his own.”** That is what sets a worked-through 6-20-14 apart. It does not stop giving. It gives in such a way that its own cup does not run dry.

On Waite’s fourteenth card the angel is alone and holds both cups. The stream between them, as Ouspensky wrote, flows both ways, and you can no longer tell which cup it is pouring into which. That is the worked-through tail: an exchange in which nobody keeps count, because there is nothing to count.

sections.h2: What this article is based on

ul: **Calculation** — the classic destiny matrix scheme with points A–T: D = A + B + C, E = A + B + C + D, M = D + E, N = D + M; every sum above 22 is reduced by adding its digits. The “sum exactly 14” rule, the constant centre 10, and the months, days and years in which the tail does not occur were checked against every day from 1900 to 2100 on the calculator’s engine. Frequencies, shares by decade and month, constant points of the chart, purposes, chakras and matches on other lines were counted over all dates from 1900 to 2025.

**Card meanings** — A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922, illustrations by Pamela Colman Smith) and Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015). Quotes from both authors are given in their original English. Numbering is the Marseille order: 8 is Justice, 11 is Strength. The remark that the Temperance picture “has no especial connexion with Temperance” comes from the first part of Waite’s book, where he discusses older decks.

**P. D. Ouspensky**, “The Symbolism of the Tarot: Philosophy of Occultism in Pictures and Numbers” (1912); we worked from the Petrograd edition of 1917, and the passage about the two cups is given in the English wording that Wen cites. The words about the narrator being unable to tell which cup the stream flows from appear only in the later, expanded edition. We checked Wen’s reference to Ouspensky on the fourteenth card against her notes.
**H. C. Andersen**, “The Little Mermaid” (1837); the quotes are our English rendering of the Russian translation by A. Hansen. The film mentioned is Disney’s The Little Mermaid (1989).
**Etymology** of the Russian zhertva follows Max Vasmer’s “Etymological Dictionary of the Russian Language”; of the English victim, the Online Etymology Dictionary.
**Do ut des** — a formula of Roman law and Roman vows. **Marcel Mauss**, “The Gift” (1925) — the three obligations of the gift.
**Drama triangle** — S. Karpman, “Fairy Tales and Script Drama Analysis”, 1968. **Winner’s triangle** — A. Choy, “The Winner’s Triangle”, 1990.

**The names “the Victim”, “the Sacrificial Soul” and “the Sacrificed Soul”, the past-life legend and the descriptions of “plus” and “minus”** come from popular destiny matrix readings. Neither Waite, nor Wen, nor Ouspensky wrote about the matrix or karmic tails: putting the three cards together into a script, the three roles, the reading of the centre and the purposes, the parallel with Andersen’s tale and the practices are the author’s interpretation.

This is an esoteric model for self-reflection, not a forecast and not a substitute for professional help. If there is violence, threats or dependency in a relationship, it is not about the tail and not about you: you need real help, not work with numbers.

paragraphs: For a couple, 6-20-14 connects the wish for agreement with the ability to bring together two sets of family habits. The Lovers at M concern closeness and shared choices; Judgement at N develops the task through relatives’ influence and ideas about family; Temperance at D focuses on dialogue and a rhythm that suits both people. We read the combination through Lisovskaya’s pair positions; the connection between the three energies is our interpretation, rather than a ready-made passage from her book.

In one family, people may drop in without warning; in the other, visits are arranged ahead. One partner experiences a spontaneous visit as warmth, the other as a disruption of personal plans. If each defends their family custom as the only caring approach, the argument quickly becomes, “Do you accept my family at all?” Judgement marks the importance of family experience, while Temperance’s task calls for a new arrangement rather than choosing which family wins.

Discuss one specific issue: visiting hours, frequency of calls, or a shared celebration. Try your own rule for the next month. Each person explains it to their own relatives on the couple’s behalf and carries some of the inconvenience of change. The difficulty is calling an arrangement a compromise when the same person always yields. Check whether both can calmly say, “Today doesn’t work,” while preserving ties with relatives and time alone together.

faq.q: What happened in a past life of someone with the 6-20-14 tail?
faq.a: Popular readings offer three versions: the soul was sacrificed in a ritual or for someone else’s plans; the person sacrificed themselves for their family, a loved one or the common good; they gave up their talent for someone else. This is a legend of the tradition: neither numbers nor cards establish events of past lives. It is more useful to read it as a description of what is already visible now: a habit of loving by giving and of waiting for what was given to be counted one day.

faq.q: Does 6-20-14 mean I will be used, or that I am doomed to be a victim?
faq.a: No. The tail is three numbers derived from a birth date. It knows nothing about the people around you and does not predict that anyone will take advantage of you. It describes a script that may repeat: giving without being asked, keeping quiet about the cost and waiting to be appreciated. Such a script changes as soon as the habits change: asking directly, naming the exchange, saying no. And if you really are being mistreated, it is not about the numbers, and the way out is not in them either.

faq.q: Is it true that people with 6-20-14 often fall ill and are prone to addiction?
faq.a: No. Popular readings say that people with this tail “get ill for attention”, that their neck, stomach and blood pressure play up and that addictions threaten them. Neither the calculation nor the cards establish such things. Three numbers know nothing about your health, and illness is neither manipulation nor punishment. If something hurts, you need a doctor, not a matrix. There is only one everyday observation worth checking on yourself: do you allow yourself rest and care while you are well, or only when you have no strength left?

faq.q: Why is the tail called “the Victim” if it has no card of sacrifice?
faq.a: In Waite’s divinatory list the word “sacrifice” belongs to the Hanged Man, the twelfth card, and it is not part of this tail. What’s more, Waite writes of the Hanged Man himself that he has been falsely called a card of martyrdom and a card of duty: the tree he hangs from is living wood, and his face **“expresses deep entrancement, not suffering”**. So true sacrifice in Waite does not need its suffering to be noticed. 6-20-14 is about something else — an exchange that has become one-sided. That is why the root of the tail is not the Hanged Man but Temperance: not learning to sacrifice better, but learning to exchange.

6-20-14 and 14-20-6 are one tail read from different ends: from the centre to the corner or from the corner to the centre. The method always writes it M–N–D: 6 is the entry, 20 the mechanism, 14 the root. There is no tail that starts with 14 or 20: the first point M is always a multiple of three. Some sites call trios like 20-6-14 “programmes”, but that is no longer a karmic tail: such numbers can stand elsewhere in the chart, and they should be read by the position they stand in.

faq.q: Are the 6-20-14 tail and the “6-20-14 programme” the same thing?
faq.a: No. A karmic tail is only the trio on the bottom ray, between the centre and the bottom corner of the chart. The same numbers can appear, for example, on the relationship line M–R1–R — in about one date in 130. Most often this happens to people with a completely different tail, 6-17-11 (for example, 15.01.1984), and less often to those with the 6-8-20 tail. There the trio describes not an old script but how a person builds closeness. The practices in this article work there too: love as an advance and waiting for gratitude look the same.

It shares its centre and mechanism with 15-20-5 — the Wheel of Fortune and Judgement — but in 15-20-5 someone else’s voice calls you to revolt, while in 6-20-14 that voice is awaited as a reward. It shares its entry with 6-8-20 — the Lovers: there the heart’s choice goes before the family’s judgement, here love waits for the judgement of the one it was given to. There is more in the section “Neighbours by number”.

faq.q: What does 6-20-14 mean in a compatibility matrix?
faq.a: In a compatibility matrix the numbers are calculated from both partners’ dates, and the trio describes the couple’s shared script, not each person’s own tail. This article is about the personal tail. If a couple gets 6-20-14, the meaning can be read with the same key. The union is tested by whether each of them sees what the other gives and whether they say it out loud. The danger for such a couple is a silent tally: one gives, the other doesn’t know they owe. The strong version is agreements made out loud about money, housework, time and concessions, and gratitude that is spoken rather than implied.

faq.q: Is 6-20-14 different for women and men?
faq.a: No. Gender plays no part in the calculation, and the meaning of the tail does not depend on it. It is easy to picture the tail as the story of a “self-sacrificing mother” or an “accommodating wife”, but those are stereotypes, not arithmetic. Anyone can be a Rescuer, a Victim or an Accuser. A man who for twenty years silently carries his family and waits for it to be appreciated is living the same tail as a woman with forty jars on someone else’s balcony.

The numbers in the matrix don’t change — what changes is how the script plays out. Signs of a worked-through tail: you ask directly and are not ashamed of it; you help when asked, or name the condition out loud; you can say no without expecting to be loved less for it; you accept gifts without handing back change at once; in a fight you don’t bring up what you once gave; you rest without a sick note. And most of all: when someone asks “how are you?”, you tell the truth before you have time to wonder whether it will sound like complaining.

report: There is praise hidden in the Russian word for sacrifice. Vasmer’s etymological dictionary groups zhertva with Lithuanian gìrti, “to praise”, Avestan gar, “praise, reward”, and Latin grātus, “pleasing, grateful”. Popular readings call the 6-20-14 tail Zhertva, “the Victim”, and explain it with a past-life legend of a sacrificed soul. The legend cannot be checked. But the script is written into the word itself: **giving — and waiting to be praised.**

The Romans had a formula for such an exchange: do ut des, “I give so that you may give”. It described contracts and vows to the gods, and there is nothing shameful in it while both sides know. **The sacrifice in this tail is a do ut des contract that only one side knows about.** The person gives and silently sets a condition. The other takes, unaware of having signed anything, until the bill arrives: “after everything I’ve done for you”.

report.h3: The judge who doesn’t know there is a trial

report: In the Waite deck a large angel appears on only three major arcana — the Lovers, Judgement and Temperance, exactly the cards of this tail. Above the Lovers the angel, in Waite’s words, is “pouring down influences”: love comes from above and need not be earned. In 6-20-14 the entry reads the other way round: love feels like a gift that must be justified. The person grows attached and starts paying at once: adapting, guessing what others want, putting their own needs aside.

Judgement holds the circle — the day when every deed is named. Every gift goes into an invisible book, to be read out loud one day. The partner will understand, the children will be grateful, the boss will see who really carried the department. The bitterest version: “when I’m dead, you’ll understand”. In Waite the trumpet does not sound from outside: the twentieth card registers transformation “in answer to the summons of the Supernal—which summons is heard and answered from within”. In this tail the trumpet has moved outside. Another person is appointed judge, and the verdict is meant to be their gratitude.

But the other does not know a trial is on, so the person passes the verdict alone. “They are ungrateful” — and the Victim becomes the Accuser. “So I didn’t give enough” — and the Victim gives even more. Wen reads reversed Judgement as an error of judgement, and both verdicts are exactly that: the contribution seems unvalued, when nobody knew of it.

The whole circle fits into one evening. She volunteered to collect her mother’s things from the dacha, the family’s country house. She hauled boxes for three hours while her brother “was busy”. That evening she phoned him: “Of course, you always have something on, and I work like a horse.” Next morning she is ashamed and offers to go alone again. Three roles in a day: Rescuer, Victim, Accuser. And nobody ever asked the brother if he was free on Saturday.

report.h3: A stream that flows both ways

report: Waite himself links the middle of the tail with its root: Judgement, he writes, “has been called truly in the past a card of eternal life, and for this reason it may be compared with that which passes under the name of Temperance”. But in Temperance, eternity is possible in this life, not after the trumpet. This is the main turn of 6-20-14: **from a reward “later” to an exchange “now”.**

The angel of Waite’s fourteenth card is “pouring the essences of life from chalice to chalice”, and holds both cups. In sacrifice the person holds one cup, their own, and pours from it into someone else’s. The other holds the second cup and decides alone whether to pour anything back. The root’s task is to take the second cup into one’s own hands. It is not someone else’s life to manage but one’s own “receiving”. Temperance here is not stinginess but the skill of mixing one’s own with others’.

In “The Symbolism of the Tarot” P. D. Ouspensky calls this card Time. His angel holds a gold and a silver cup, and the Voice explains: “One of the cups the angel holds is the past, the other is the future. The rainbow stream between the cups is the present. You see that it flows both ways.” **In sacrifice it is always clear which way it flows: from me to you. In Temperance there is no telling — the stream flows both ways.**

report.h3: The voice the little mermaid gave away first

report: The parallel is ours, not the method’s tradition. At the start of Andersen’s “The Little Mermaid” the grandmother names an exchange where nobody loses anything: “He will give you a soul and keep his own.” The little mermaid hears something else — a soul can be bought — and gives the sea witch her voice first. Then the whole circle: every step like treading on sharp knives, and a prince who loves her “only as one loves a dear, good child”. He tells her about the girl who supposedly saved him, and she sighs to herself: “Alas! He doesn’t know that it was I who saved his life!”

The judgement comes, but the verdict goes to another: the prince recognises his rescuer in the visiting princess. Even “when I’m dead, you’ll understand” comes true to the letter: next morning the prince and his bride gaze at the sea foam “as if they knew that the little mermaid had thrown herself into the waves”. And nothing changes.

Every child who finishes the tale asks why she didn’t write to the prince. Andersen gives no answer. The tail does: a Victim doesn’t tell, but waits for others to guess. In 1989 Disney rewrote the ending, and it is happy for one reason: the mermaid gets her voice back, and by it the prince knows who saved him.

report.h3: A cup that never runs dry

report: The way out is in the same picture of Temperance. Asking means holding out one’s own cup. Giving means pouring into someone else’s. Setting limits means knowing when to stop the stream. In daily life that means three habits:

ul: list what was given unasked over the past year and what is silently expected back, then decide line by line: ask out loud or call it a gift;
one direct request a day: “I need… Can you…?” — no preamble, no “if it’s not too much trouble”;
name the exchange before helping: “This is a gift, I don’t need anything” — and truly expect nothing; or “I’ll help with the move, and on Saturday you look after my kids”.

report: If someone is a victim in the literal sense — of violence, threats, humiliation, financial control — it is not about the tail. It is not a lesson but a situation that calls for real help: from loved ones, a lawyer, a psychologist, a crisis line.

In the worked-through version the person loves seriously and generously, and notices and names what others contribute — the very thing they once waited for. Others feel lighter around them: they give exactly what is needed, not everything for everyone. The grandmother’s formula comes true: **such a person gives a soul and keeps their own.** Between the cups the stream flows so that nobody can tell which pours into which: an exchange where nobody keeps count, because there is nothing to count.
